headline: Jumbo blues crash Jersey inlets as bay water hits 68 degrees
subhead: Raritan Bay stripers still thick on bunker while fluke fishing heats up from Shark River to Cape May.
body_markdown:
The water's finally talking our language down here, and the fish are listening loud and clear. Bay temps hit 68 degrees this week — a solid four-degree jump from the ocean side — and that thermal gradient is stacking bait like you wouldn't believe. The bunker are thick from Sandy Hook to Shark River, and everything with teeth is having a field day.

Raritan Bay is absolutely loaded with stripers right now. I'm talking about fish from schoolies to solid 30-inchers crushing peanut bunker on the flood tide. The key is finding those temperature breaks where the warmer bay water meets the cooler ocean flow. Fish the edges with live bunker on a fishfinder rig, or throw 6-inch white Hogy soft plastics on 3/4-ounce jig heads. The bass are sitting in 15 to 20 feet, ambushing bait as it gets swept through the channel. Best action has been two hours before and after the tide change.

But here's the real story — the bluefish have returned in force, and I mean the jumbo choppers we haven't seen in years. Manasquan Inlet has been producing blues in the 8 to 12-pound class, fish that'll test your drag and your patience. They're hitting everything from metal jigs to fresh bunker chunks. I've been running 4-inch chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets on 1-ounce bucktails, bouncing them through the inlet on the outgoing water. The blues are stacked up where the current rips around the jetties, waiting for bait to get flushed out of the back bay.

Fluke fishing has turned the corner too. Shark River has been consistent for keepers in the 18 to 22-inch range, with fish holding in the deeper holes on the incoming tide. The trick is working 5-inch white Gulp baits on 3/8-ounce jig heads, keeping them moving slow along the bottom. The fluke are feeding on the abundant spearing and small crabs that the warmer water has brought inshore. I've been finding the best action in 8 to 12 feet of water, especially around the marina docks where the structure holds bait.

Down at Barnegat, the inlet has been producing a mixed bag of blues, fluke, and even some early weakfish. The weakies are small — mostly 12 to 14-inchers — but they're a welcome sight after years of poor numbers. Pink Gulp on light jig heads has been the ticket, fished on the edges of the channel where the current slows.

The water clarity has been excellent despite some afternoon thunderstorms. That 68-degree reading in the bay is crucial — it's warm enough to fire up the baitfish but not so hot that it pushes the gamefish deep. The gradient between bay and ocean water is creating perfect ambush points at every inlet from Sandy Hook to Cape May.

Looking ahead, we're coming up on the new moon Friday, which means spring tides and serious current flow. That's going to flush even more bait out of the back bays and concentrate the predators at the inlet mouths. I'm expecting the bluefish bite to get even better as those big tides move more food around. The stripers should stay active as long as the bunker schools hold, and with water temps climbing toward 70, we might start seeing some early summer species like Spanish mackerel showing up in the mix.

This is prime time Jersey fishing — multiple species, aggressive fish, and conditions that are only going to get better. Get out there before the weekend crowds hit the water.
